definition: To give machine output a final pass by hand; the human coat of care that turns generated into made.
etymology: From furniture-making, where machine-cut pieces are hand-finished — sanded, fitted, signed. Both halves are old: hand is Old English hand, unchanged; finish is fourteenth-century, via Old French finir from Latin finire, ‘to bound, to end’. The compound is the young one: cabinetmakers, tailors, bookbinders and gunsmiths have marked work hand-finished since machines began doing the roughing-out, and the label always meant the same thing — a machine did the bulk of it, and a person did the part that had to be trusted. The word was built to sit on a small brass plate, and it still reads like one.
in_use: Ship nothing raw. Everything gets a handfinish, even the emails.
the_case: Without a name, the last pass registers as overhead: a tax on using the machine at all, paid grudgingly, skipped when you are tired. Name it and it flips. A handfinish is not the tax; it is the stage where the value gets added, and skipping it stops being efficiency and becomes shipping unsanded furniture. Note what the definition does not say. It does not say better. Machine output that gets handfinished was often already good; that is precisely why the word is useful and rewrite is not. It names the smaller, humbler claim — that between generated and made there is a threshold, and someone chose to walk the work across it. The word works twice: as a verb it is the act, as a noun the quality the act leaves behind. The machine cuts. You sign.
seo_title: handfinish — the human pass that turns generated into made
seo_description: It's fine, but it reads produced, not written. Handfinish names the final pass by hand that turns machine output into made work — and who touched it last.
